claims.text: Factory's Missions architecture uses three roles (orchestrator, workers, validators); the orchestrator plans, decomposes and steers but delegates all investigation and implementation to avoid accumulating granular context.

In Missions, the orchestrator writes a validation contract, a finite checklist of testable behavioral assertions, before defining any features so the contract is not contaminated by the planned implementation.

Missions scrutiny validators review each worker's implementation and trajectory, while user-testing validators exercise the system as a black box against the validation contract; validators surface issues to the orchestrator rather than fixing them.

A single Missions run that built a Slack clone took 16.5 hours (2.3% orchestration, 60.5% implementation, 37.2% validation), used 185 agent runs and 778.5M tokens, and produced 38.8k lines of code, 52.5% of them tests, at 89.25% statement coverage.

Missions execution is serial, with parallelism allowed only for read-only work such as codebase search, API research and code review, because parallel agents conflict, duplicate work and make inconsistent architectural decisions.

Custom droids (subagents) are Markdown files in .factory/droids/ that run in a fresh context window per invocation via the Task tool, with complexity tiers (light/medium/heavy), background execution returning a task_id, and a resume option; built-ins include worker and read-only explorer.

Factory's context stack layers repository overviews, semantic search, targeted file-system reads, enterprise integrations (e.g. Sentry, Notion, Google Docs) and hierarchical User Memory and Org Memory, motivated by Chroma's Context Rot finding that performance degrades as input length grows.

In Factory's December 2025 compression study over 36,611 messages, Factory's structured summarization scored 3.70 overall versus Anthropic 3.44 and OpenAI 3.35, with artifact tracking the weakest dimension at 2.45.

Droid 1.0 made programmatic 'script mode' the default, where the model writes JavaScript run in a sandbox that calls tools; the base prompt shrank 37% to 13,055 tokens and only two tool definitions ship up front, down from 11.
Factory's illustrative case of moving and verifying 151 Linear issues took 312 tool calls and now needs 2 requests and 61K tokens, versus about 36 requests and 3.1M input tokens before.

Factory Environments are reusable sandbox definitions built into portable images ahead of time, rebuilt every few hours and validated, with only successful builds promoted so Droids never start from a faulty environment.

Droid Computers are persistent managed or bring-your-own machines that retain filesystem, credentials, services and process memory across sessions; managed ones are 4 CPU, 8GB RAM and auto-pause when idle.

OpenCompute is a self-hosted orchestrator in private preview that connects outbound to Factory over TLS WebSocket, using a Go control plane with Postgres state, a reconciler, immutable Builds and gRPC provider drivers, so Droid sandboxes can run in a customer's VPC.

An independent sandbox analysis found the Droid CLI has no built-in OS-level isolation, its project-directory write restriction is enforced by the agent rather than the OS, and hooks and MCP stdio servers run with the user's credentials.
Droid's autonomy levels (Off, Low, Medium, High) set the highest-risk action allowed without approval; Missions orchestration requires High autonomy or --skip-permissions-unsafe.
Code Droid scored 19.27% on SWE-bench Full and 31.67% pass@1 on SWE-bench Lite in June 2024, with token use up to 13 million per patch.

In Code Droid's SWE-bench failure analysis, 8% of tasks never had the target file in the analysed set, another 8% had it outside the top-5 ranking, and 6% had it top-ranked but not selected for editing.

In September 2025 Factory reported Droid at 58.75% on Terminal-Bench Core, first place, with Droid+Opus 4.1 at 58.8% versus Claude Code+Opus at 43.2% and Droid+GPT-5 at 52.5% versus Codex CLI at 42.8%.
On Snorkel's independent Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard, Droid with GPT-5.3-Codex ranks 10th at 77.3% ±2.2, against a top score of 84.7%.
On Terminal-Bench 4 (Droid 1.0, October 2026), Droid scored 65.2% with Claude Opus 5.5 versus Cursor and OpenCode 62.1%, Devin 59.6% and Claude Code 57.6%.
The Terminal-Bench 4 head-to-head numbers for Droid 1.0 are all self-reported by Factory.
Vals AI's independent SWE-bench Verified listing places 'GPT 5.5 / Factory' at 76.20%, ranked 41st, well below the 97.00% top entry.
Factory Router reportedly retains 99% of Claude Opus 4.7's pass rate at 20% lower cost per session on Terminal-Bench 2, while the most aggressive routing dropped pass rate to 81% at 56% of Opus cost.

Factory's Droid Review automation triggers on PR open, synchronize, reopen and ready-for-review, skips drafts, posts inline comments on bugs such as null dereferences, race conditions and injection, and approves when no issues are found, deliberately skipping style opinions.
Factory reports Droid reviewed 99.5% of mergeable pull requests with engineers resolving 81% of its comments.
